summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer Simulator

We developed an interactive simulator called Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, designed to introduce children and young people to the world of space exploration through a fun and engaging learning experience.

Our project aims to transform space mission concepts into an interactive experience where participants can learn, explore, and become familiar with the challenges of being an astronaut. To develop it, we used Claude as our main coding assistant, Gemini to enhance and refine the simulator with additional details, and ChatGPT to structure and improve our project pitch.

This project is important because it encourages curiosity about science, technology, and space exploration, making learning more accessible, interactive, and inspiring for the next generation of explorers.
details:
Mission Zero-G: Junior Astronaut Simulator

What it does and how it works
Mission Zero-G is a first-person 3D space game that runs in the browser. The player gets a call sign, picks a destination (Mercury, Venus, the Moon, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Neptune) and learns how much they would weigh there. For example, on Venus a 35 kg student would weigh 31.6 kg. The mission has three stages: (1) grab the detector and board the rocket, (2) travel and survive in-flight emergencies, repairing failures caused by a corrupted signal using real science, and (3) land in the green beam, study the world and transmit the data. At the end, players get a science sheet and an astronaut certificate.

Benefits

  • It makes abstract physics, like gravity and weight vs. mass, something students feel by playing.
  • It needs no installation, account or special hardware. It opens in any modern browser, so it works in classrooms with limited resources.
  • Each planet has different gravity, which encourages replay and comparison between worlds.
  • Real-time setbacks make students think, react and apply what they learn, which helps them retain it better than passive content.

Intended impact
We want to spark curiosity about space science in students and show them that NASA’s open data is something they can explore and build with. Our goal is that every player finishes a mission knowing how gravity changes from world to world and feeling like a junior astronaut.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: gravity values and planetary information from NASA’s Planetary Fact Sheets (NASA open data).
  • 3D engine: Three.js, running in the web browser, with JavaScript, HTML and CSS.
  • AI: Claude (Anthropic’s AI assistant) was used to help design, code and build the entire project, including the game logic, the interface, the written content and the video pitch. The only element not made with AI is the voice in our video pitch, which is our own.
  • Hardware: standard laptops; no special hardware needed.

Creativity
Unlike other educational space projects, Mission Zero-G does not just present information: it challenges the player in real time. During the mission, unexpected problems and setbacks appear, such as failures caused by a corrupted signal, that make it hard to complete the mission. To overcome them, players must apply real science, so they learn by doing and not by reading. This turns NASA’s open planetary data into a story the player lives through, with a call sign, emergencies to solve, a landing and a final certificate. It encourages learning, keeps players engaged and benefits every user by making science feel like an adventure.

Factors our team considered

  • Accessibility: browser-based, free and light enough for school laptops.
  • Scientific accuracy: all gravity values come from NASA’s fact sheets.
  • Audience: young students, so we designed short missions, clear objectives and simple controls.
  • Engagement: progress and rewards, such as a science sheet and a certificate, that motivate replay.
  • Learning through challenge: difficulty comes from real-time obstacles that require applying science.
